interactive.title: Two receipts and a grid
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on a grid of guesses. Its two axes are the two unknowns of a story, such as a drink's price across and a bag of popcorn's price up, in pounds, or a and b in a machine's law P = aW + b. The guess is a ring you drag anywhere on the grid. It snaps to set steps, 50p on most price screens. Beside the grid, each fact in the story is a receipt card. It puts the guess into its own rule, such as 2 × d + p for 2 drinks and 1 bag of popcorn, and shows the total that guess would make. It shows ✓ when that matches the real total, and too much or too little when it does not. On a puzzle each card keeps its rule back, showing Its equation: ?, until you check an answer or ask Why?, because turning the words into equations is the puzzle. Each guess a receipt accepts leaves a small mark. The marks line up, because every pair that makes a rule come to its total lies on that rule's straight line, so the receipt's line is drawn through them, receipt 1's solid and receipt 2's dashed. Where two lines cross, only the crossing point is on both, so only that guess gets two ticks. A receipt that is another one doubled lays its line on top of the first. One whose total does not fit runs parallel and never crosses it. Beneath the grid the working runs line by line: the letters and what they stand for, one equation per fact, the solve, the check in the story, and what the pair means, with units. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. A puzzle shows a story and three answers. A wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? shows the working and the check in the story.
interactive.ignores: The prices, orders and machine readings are example figures, chosen to give tidy answers, not real prices or a real machine's readings. Guesses snap to set steps, so the marks are only some of the guesses a receipt accepts; its line holds every pair in between too. Real machine readings scatter a little, so two readings give a law that depends on which two you pick. Straight-line graphs fitted a line through many readings for that reason.

explain.text:
Each fact a story gives about two unknowns can be written as one equation, so two separate facts give two equations, and the pair that solves them is the answer that fits the whole story. Take a cinema receipt: 2 drinks and 1 bag of popcorn cost £8. Call a drink's price d and a bag of popcorn's p, both in pounds. Each item's count times its price, added up, makes the total, so the receipt says 2d + p = 8. It can check any guess by working out 2 × d + p and comparing it with £8. It accepts a £2 drink with £4 popcorn, because 4 + 4 = 8. It accepts £3 and £2, and £1 and £6, too. For each drink price just one popcorn price makes £8, and each £1 more on the drink must come off as £2 less on the popcorn. That steady step is why, on the grid of guesses with d across and p up, every guess it accepts lands on one straight line, the line of 2d + p = 8. One fact about two unknowns allows endless answers,[^1] so on its own it cannot tell you the prices.

A second receipt says 1 drink and 2 bags of popcorn cost £7, so d + 2p = 7. Its accepted guesses, such as £1 and £3 or £5 and £1, make a second line. A guess that passes one receipt can fail the other: £2 and £4 make 2 + 8 = 10 on the second, not 7. Only the crossing point, a £3 drink and £2 popcorn, passes both receipts: 2 × 3 + 2 = 8 and 3 + 2 × 2 = 7. That pair is the solution, because it makes both equations true.[^2] Dragging guesses about finds it only one guess at a time, and only when the answer falls on a grid mark, so work it out instead. The first receipt gives p = 8 − 2d. Swap that into the second: d + 2(8 − 2d) = 7, so d + 16 − 4d = 7, −3d = −9 and d = −9 ÷ −3 = 3. Then p = 8 − 6 = 2.

The steps are the same for any story. Say what you are looking for, and give each unknown a letter,[^3] written down with what it stands for and its unit. Turn each fact into one equation.[^3] Solve the pair by substitution or elimination. Check the answer in the story's own words, and say what it means, with units. The unknowns need not be prices. In Straight-line graphs you read a lifting machine's law, P = aW + b, off a graph, where P is the effort and W the load. Two readings give it by algebra instead. Say a load of 100 N needs an effort of 15 N, and 300 N needs 35 N. Now a and b are the unknowns, so each reading gives one equation: 100a + b = 15 and 300a + b = 35. Take the first away from the second: 200a = 20, so a = 0.1, and b = 15 − 10 = 5. The law is P = 0.1W + 5. Each extra newton of load needs 0.1 N more effort, and 5 N is the effort with no load on. The Second Engineer exam's maths syllabus asks for just this: equations of two unknowns built from the data in a question, then solved.[^4]

The second fact must say something new. A receipt for 4 drinks and 2 bags of popcorn at £16 is the first receipt doubled, so it accepts every guess the first accepts: a £1 drink and £6 popcorn make 4 + 12 = 16. Its line lies on top of the first, and there are endless answers.[^5] At £14 it would disagree with the first receipt. Its line would run parallel, and no pair would fit both.[^6] **Two separate facts about the same two unknowns give two equations,[^3] and when their lines cross, the pair that solves them, checked in the story, is the one answer that fits both facts.**

analogy.text: A navigator takes a compass bearing on one lighthouse. That one fact puts the ship somewhere along one line on the chart, as one receipt allows a whole line of prices. A bearing on a second lighthouse gives a second line, and the ship is where the two lines cross, as two receipts pin down one pair of prices.
analogy.breaks: Real bearings carry small errors, so navigators often take a third as a check, and the three lines make a small triangle rather than a point. Two exact facts in a story pin the pair exactly when their lines cross. And a chart's lines are places on the sea, while the grid's lines are lists of possible answers.

practice.text:
- Read the story and say what you are looking for.
- Give each unknown a letter and write down what it stands for, with its unit, such as d = the price of a drink, in £.
- Write one equation for each fact. For a bill, each item's count times its price, added up, makes the total.
- Check the two facts are separate. If one is the other scaled up, there are endless answers. If the left sides match once scaled but the totals do not, there is no answer.
- Solve the pair: usually substitution when one fact already says what a letter equals, elimination otherwise.
- Check the pair in every fact of the story, in its own words.
- Say what each number means, with its unit.

**Rule of thumb:** one letter for each unknown, written down with its meaning and unit before any equation. Two unknowns need two separate facts.

**Worked example:** two orders from a wholesaler, with example prices. Order 1 is 10 m of 2.5 mm² cable and 10 m of 1.5 mm², for £20. Order 2 is 10 m of 2.5 mm² and 20 m of 1.5 mm², for £28. Let x be the price of the 2.5 mm² and y the price of the 1.5 mm², both in £ a metre. Then 10x + 10y = 20 and 10x + 20y = 28. Take the first away from the second: 10y = 8, so y = 0.8. Put it back: 10x + 8 = 20, so 10x = 12 and x = 1.2. Check in the story: 10 m at £1.20 and 10 m at 80p make £12 + £8 = £20, and 10 m at £1.20 and 20 m at 80p make £12 + £16 = £28. So the 2.5 mm² costs £1.20 a metre and the 1.5 mm² costs 80p a metre.

**Common mistakes**
- Using one fact only. A £2 drink and £4 popcorn fit the first receipt, but make £10 on the second, not £7.
- Stopping at the numbers. Say what each one means, with its unit.

**Slips to check for**
- Swapping which letter stands for which thing. Write the meanings down first.
- Writing 2 bags of popcorn as p + 2 instead of 2p.
- Taking the same fact twice, such as a receipt that is another one doubled. It adds nothing new.
- Forcing a machine's law through zero. P = aW + b has an effort b with no load on, so one reading's P ÷ W is not a unless b is 0.

sources.quote: To solve a system of two linear equations, we want to find the values of the variables that are solutions to both equations. In other words, we are looking for the ordered pairs that make both equations true.

sources.title: Solving simultaneous equations graphically - KS3 Maths - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: If the two lines cross, then the coordinates of this intersection are the solutions to the simultaneous equations. If the lines are parallel (and therefore do not intersect), there is no solution.

interactive.html:
A grid of guesses at two unknown prices, and receipts that each check a guess with their own rule. Every story here uses example figures.

Drag the ring, or use the arrow keys, to try any guess on the grid.
interactive.title: Two receipts and a grid
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is every guess one receipt accepts landing on one line, and only the crossing of two receipts' lines passing both, when you drag the guess around the grid.

checks.label: Equations that have more than one unknown can have an infinite number of solutions: every receipt, order, reading and fact here accepts at least three guesses on its grid, and every guess it accepts lies on its one straight line

A solution of a system of two equations is an ordered pair that makes both equations true: in every two-fact story here exactly one guess on the grid passes both facts, and it is where their two lines cross
When the two equations were really the same line, there were infinitely many solutions: receipt 3 at £16 accepts exactly the guesses receipt 1 accepts, and its line lies on top of receipt 1's

If the lines are parallel (and therefore do not intersect), there is no solution: at £14 receipt 3's line, and 6 drinks and 3 bags at £21, run alongside receipt 1's without meeting it, and no guess on the grid passes both

Every worked line is right, by hand: p = 8 − 2d swapped in gives d + 16 − 4d = 7, −3d = −9, d = −9 ÷ −3 = 3 and p = 2; p = 6.50 − 2d gives −3d = −7.50, a £2.50 drink and £1.50 popcorn; 10y = 8 gives 80p and £1.20 a metre; 4w = 16 and a £3.50 socket; 200a = 20 gives P = 0.1W + 5; 300a = 24 gives a = 0.08 and b = 10; 2x = 24 gives 12 m and 18 m; and 35 N at 250 N

Every puzzle has three answers, one of them right, and a hint of its own for each wrong one; the right pair passes both facts, each wrong pair fails at least one, and only the right second receipt crosses receipt 1

Before an answer a puzzle keeps back each card's equation, the crossing ring and the working; a right answer or Why? draws both lines, rings the crossing, moves the guess there so both cards match, and works it through; a wrong pair is tried in every card and fails one

The first screen opens with a £2 drink and £4 popcorn on receipt 1, where 2 × 2 + 4 = 8 matches; its demonstration leaves marks at (£2, £4), (£3, £2) and (£1, £6) and only then draws the line through them

On the doubled-receipt screen receipt 3 at £16 accepts a £1 drink and £6 popcorn and its line lies on receipt 1's; at £14 the same guess comes to too much, its line moves off to run alongside, and no ring appears
Every demonstration settles within its 3 to 5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends, and a puzzle's answer, Why? or wrong pick settles within 2.5 s

applied.problem: "Only the crossing point ... gets two ticks" is stated for every screen, but on the doubled-receipt screen (step 8) the lines lie on top of each other, so every guess on that line gets two ticks; narrow it to screens where the lines cross.
